title: Managing Self-Learning Experts under Per-Round Budget Constraints
claim: Our budgeted expert-manager achieves lower cumulative loss than baselines and concentrates its selection and learning effort on the best experts.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, line plot then two grouped bar charts, shared legend below
description: Three side-by-side plots share one legend at the bottom. Panel (a) shows cumulative loss against steps (0 to 25000) as dotted and dashed lines with markers and shaded confidence bands. Blue lines are M-LCB, red lines are LimitedAdvice, and a black dotted line is SmoothCORRAL. Lighter shades mark larger budgets M=1 to 4. The black SmoothCORRAL curve is highest, and the light blue M-LCB curves are lowest. Panel (b) is a grouped bar chart of arm selection counts over arm indices 0 to 9. Selections concentrate on arm 0 and fall off for later arms. Panel (c) is a grouped bar chart of optimization counts per arm. Blue bars are skewed toward the first arms, while red LimitedAdvice bars stay spread across later arms. Gray gridlines run through all three panels.
caption: Performance comparison on the MAB model selection. (a) Cumulative Loss. (b) Final distribution of arm selection. (c) Allocation of computational budget across arms.
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of sequential decision-making under learning budget constraints. Such settings naturally arise in applications like managing a portfolio of bandit or reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. We propose a novel UCB-type algorithm, M-LCB, designed to manage a pool of $K$ self-learning experts in a stochastic environment while accounting for a limited per-round learning budget $M$. At each round, M-LCB selects one expert to make a decision and at most $M \le K$ experts to learn. For selection, M-LCB uses confidence bounds constructed from limited prior knowledge about the experts (i.e., mild assumptions) and their observed training losses. We derive anytime regret bounds for M-LCB that scale with the individual regrets of the experts. In particular, if each expert has regret $\tilde O(T^Î±)$ by round $T$, then M-LCB guarantees an overall regret of $\tilde O\left(\sqrt{KT/M} + (K/M)^{1-Î±}T^Î±\right)$ relative to the best expert in hindsight. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of M-LCB using self-learning experts instantiated as (i) parametric models and (ii) bandit algorithms.
